home.eyebrow: Respiratory Neurodynamics · Universidad Autónoma de Chile
home.title: Neural and glial control of breathing
home.introduction: We investigate how brainstem neurons and astrocytes regulate breathing, and how these signals relate to physiology, cognition, and disease.
home.heroImageAlt: Immunofluorescence micrograph from the lab showing green, red, cyan, and blue signals against a black background.

publicEntry.title: Breathing feels automatic. For the brain, it is a task coordinated second by second.
publicEntry.introduction: As we sleep, walk, or exercise, the body’s needs change. Brain circuits receive that information and adjust the breathing rhythm without requiring conscious thought.
body: Part of this work takes place in the brainstem, where neurons and astrocytes participate in networks that generate and modulate breathing. Dr. Esteban Díaz Jara studies how these cells coordinate and how their signals relate to respiratory, cardiovascular, and brain activity.

The laboratory examines what changes during intermittent hypoxia or after ischemic brain injury. To follow the process from the cell to the whole organism, it combines physiology, electrophysiology, microscopy, and data analysis.
publicEntry.question: How does coordination among cells and respiratory circuits change before disruption becomes visible across the whole organism?
publicEntry.glossaryLabel: Three concepts for reading this site

glossary.definition: The region linking the brain and spinal cord, involved in essential automatic functions, including breathing.
A glial cell that maintains the neuronal environment and also participates in communication within neural circuits.
An experimental system used to test a biological mechanism; its results do not translate directly to what occurs in patients.

publicEntry.scope: These studies seek to understand biological mechanisms. They do not provide diagnoses or medical advice, and a hypothesis remains identified as such until evidence allows it to be evaluated.

home.researchTitle: Three questions organizing our current work
home.researchIntroduction: From cellular mechanisms to cognition, we study how breathing is generated, how it synchronizes other brain networks, and what changes in disease.

researchAreas.title: How breathing rhythm is generated and regulated
researchAreas.summary: We study how neurons and astrocytes generate and regulate breathing rhythm and cardiorespiratory homeostasis.
researchAreas.body: We study how neurons and astrocytes in nuclei such as the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), the preBötzinger complex, the Kölliker-Fuse nucleus, and the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) generate and regulate breathing rhythm and cardiorespiratory homeostasis. A particular focus of our work is the role of NTS astrocytes as active modulators, and not merely support cells, in the emergence of respiratory disorders during chronic intermittent hypoxia and following cortical ischemic stroke.
researchAreas.imageAlt: Immunofluorescence micrograph acquired in the lab and shown in the fluorophores’ original colors.
researchAreas.figureCaption: Immunofluorescence micrograph acquired by the lab. Channels are shown in their original acquisition colors; anatomy and scale will be documented with the associated experimental record.
researchAreas.question: Which neuronal and astrocytic mechanisms sustain breathing rhythm and cardiorespiratory homeostasis?
researchAreas.hypothesis: Astrocytes in respiratory nuclei actively regulate the circuit and contribute to its dysfunction in disease.

researchAreas.title: How breathing synchronizes brain networks
researchAreas.summary: We investigate how respiratory oscillations synchronize cortical and hippocampal circuits.
researchAreas.body: Breathing does more than maintain homeostasis: it also organizes brain activity. We investigate how respiratory oscillations synchronize cortical and hippocampal circuits, and how this synchronization relates to cognition, sleep, and learning. In our models of chronic intermittent hypoxia and ischemic stroke, we seek to understand how astrocyte-mediated dysfunction in brainstem respiratory nuclei reshapes connectivity across these circuits.
researchAreas.imageAlt: Fluorescence image produced by the lab, with scientific signals displayed against a dark background.
researchAreas.figureCaption: Fluorescence image produced by the lab. The multichannel acquisition is preserved; interpretation depends on the preparation and markers used in each experiment.
researchAreas.question: How do respiratory oscillations couple with cortical and hippocampal activity?
researchAreas.hypothesis: Respiratory dynamics provide a temporal reference for brain networks involved in sleep, learning, and cognition.

researchAreas.title: What changes in disease
researchAreas.summary: We examine the two-way relationship between brain alterations, respiratory function, physiology, and cognition.
researchAreas.body: Brain alterations can profoundly modify respiratory function, while respiratory dysfunction can, in turn, worsen the course of disease. We work with two models that address this bidirectional relationship: chronic intermittent hypoxia and cortical ischemic stroke. In both, we focus on how astrocyte-mediated alterations in respiratory nuclei affect physiology and cognition.
researchAreas.imageAlt: Multichannel micrograph from the lab showing fluorescent signals against a black background.
researchAreas.figureCaption: Multichannel micrograph acquired by the lab. It is presented as an experimental record without assigning markers or regions not confirmed in its metadata.
researchAreas.question: How do breathing, brain activity, and disease progression modify one another?
researchAreas.hypothesis: Glial alterations in respiratory nuclei may connect cardiorespiratory dysfunction with brain and cognitive changes.

research.title: Respiratory circuits, astrocytes, and disease
research.introduction: We investigate how brainstem respiratory circuits interact with the brain networks that sustain physiology, behavior, and disease. Our work is organized around three complementary questions, moving from cellular mechanisms to their impact on brain function.

techniques.title: Experimental design and methodological capabilities
techniques.introduction: We organize our capabilities around the actual progression of scientific work: we generate and manipulate models, measure physiology, visualize cells and circuits, and analyze the resulting data.

stages.title: Models and causality
stages.description: We generate disease models and manipulate specific circuits to test causal relationships among astrocytes, respiratory circuits, and disease.
stages.scope: Preclinical models of chronic intermittent hypoxia and cortical ischemic stroke.
stages.output: Defined perturbations for testing causal relationships in circuits and cell populations.

stages.title: Physiology in real time
stages.description: We record respiratory, cardiorespiratory, and brain activity at high temporal resolution in awake animals.
stages.scope: Awake animals, cardiorespiratory recordings, and 32-channel multichannel LFP.
stages.output: Synchronized time series of ventilation, cardiovascular variables, and neuronal activity.

stages.title: Cells and circuits
stages.description: We identify and characterize, in vitro, the cell populations involved in respiratory circuits.
stages.scope: Immunofluorescence-labelled tissue and brain slices for in vitro studies.
stages.output: Cell distribution, morphology, and calcium signals in defined cells and circuits.

stages.title: Signals and structure
stages.description: We extract interpretable structure from electrophysiological signals, images, and gene-expression data.
stages.scope: Electrophysiological signals, images, and gene-expression data.
stages.output: Reproducible metrics, temporal relationships, and interpretable multivariate patterns.

techniques.closingText: By integrating in vivo physiology, microscopy, electrophysiology, and computational analysis, we can connect cellular changes with cardiorespiratory patterns and brain activity.

team.title: Research team
team.introduction: The team includes researchers and students trained in physiology, neurobiology, microscopy, and data analysis.

members.name: Esteban Díaz Jara
members.credentials: Biochemist · Ph.D. in Biological Sciences, Physiology
bio: Esteban trained as a biochemist at Universidad Austral de Chile in Valdivia. He completed his undergraduate thesis under Felipe Barros at the Centro de Estudios Científicos (CECs), where he studied neuronal energy metabolism. He later moved to Santiago and worked with Juan Andrés Orellana on connexin- and pannexin-mediated glia–neuron communication.

In 2019, he entered the Ph.D. program in Biological Sciences, with a specialization in Physiology, at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. Under Rodrigo Del Río’s supervision, his doctoral research examined how astrocytic glutamate transporters in the retrotrapezoid nucleus contribute to central chemoreflex potentiation and respiratory disturbances in a model of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

In mid-2025, he joined the Institute of Biomedical Sciences at Universidad Autónoma de Chile as an investigator and associate professor. In parallel, he is conducting postdoctoral research under Professor Rodrigo Iturriaga’s supervision.
members.research: His work integrates cardiorespiratory physiology, astrocyte signaling, and circuit dynamics to understand how breathing interacts with the brain in health and disease.

members.name: Sinay C. Vicencio Orellana
members.credentials: Biochemist · M.Sc. in Biological Sciences · Ph.D. candidate in Physiological Sciences
bio: Sinay is the lab manager of the Respiratory Neurodynamics Laboratory, led by Dr. Esteban Díaz Jara. Her background spans neurobiology and preclinical models of central nervous system myelin disorders, cardiorespiratory physiology, and translational medicine, with a particular interest in preventive medicine for healthy aging.
In the lab, she combines logistics and experimental planning with hands-on work in molecular biology, physiology, and microscopy. She also coordinates project priorities and experimental schedules.
members.research: She coordinates the lab’s scientific operations and contributes to molecular biology, physiology, and microscopy experiments.

philosophy.title: How we record, review, and learn
philosophy.introduction: Operational criteria for recording data, reviewing results, training researchers, and coordinating experimental work.
philosophy.statement: Honesty with data, one’s own work, and the team is a central principle of the laboratory. We maintain high standards and recognize that scientific training requires time, supervision, and progressive autonomy. Curiosity and critical self-reflection guide experimental design and the interpretation of results. Each member develops an individual project with personal responsibility and day-to-day collaboration; mistakes are analyzed to correct procedures and support learning.
philosophy.mission: To investigate how brainstem respiratory circuits interact with brain networks in order to understand physiology, behavior, and disease, while training researchers who are honest, independent, self-critical, and able to work as part of a team.
philosophy.vision: To consolidate a respiratory neurodynamics research program in Latin America that produces reproducible knowledge and trains researchers who are principled, independent, and rigorous.

values.title: Honesty
values.description: We record expected and unexpected results, preserve original data, and report deviations from protocol.

values.title: Curiosity
values.description: New questions become explicit hypotheses, possible controls, and interpretation criteria before the experiment.

values.title: Critical self-reflection
values.description: We review assumptions, controls, and analyses before assigning an observed difference to the mechanism under study.

values.title: Responsibility
values.description: Each member documents their work, anticipates experimental risks, and communicates changes in commitments early.

values.title: Teamwork
values.description: Protocols, decisions, and difficulties are shared so that knowledge does not depend on one person.

values.title: Rigor and progressive development
values.description: Autonomy increases with demonstrated experience; supervision and review are adjusted to each training stage.

values.title: Learning from mistakes
values.description: Errors are recorded, their cause is examined, and corrections are incorporated into the protocol or analysis workflow.
